narrative:
The model predicted a 57.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year in law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. This lower standing signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score of 35.5 worked in the opposite direction, modestly pulling the prediction toward passing. While helpful, it was not strong enough to overcome the effect of your class rank. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.5 also nudged the outcome toward success. In fact, it was higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students, yet this positive signal was still outweighed by the third-year class rank.

Taken together, the model concluded that your overall profile indicated a greater than even chance of failing the bar on the first try, which led to the rejection.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your class rank in the remaining part of law school if possible, or consider retaking the LSAT to raise that score further. Strengthening either of those two areas would most directly improve your chances in a future application.
